whatsThis.passwords: A private list of your logins. Only you can open it — everything is scrambled, so even someone holding the file can't read it.
whatsThis.notes: A safe place for text you want kept private — recovery codes, secret numbers, personal notes. It stays hidden until you reveal it.
whatsThis.cards: Store your card details so you don't have to memorise them. They stay locked and masked until you tap to reveal.
whatsThis.generator: Builds strong, random passwords for you — the kind that are almost impossible to guess or crack.
whatsThis.audit: A quick health check. It flags passwords that are weak, reused, or old, so you know exactly what to improve.
whatsThis.import-export: Bring passwords in from another app, or save a copy out. Your data is always yours to move.
whatsThis.keys: You have a pair of keys: one you share so people can send you locked files, and one you keep secret to open them. This is where you look after both.
whatsThis.encrypt: Turn any file into a locked version only the right person can open — perfect for sharing something private.
whatsThis.encrypt-file: Turn any file into a locked version only the right person can open — perfect for sharing something private.
whatsThis.encrypt-directory: Same idea as locking a file, but for a whole folder — everything is bundled and locked into one protected file.
whatsThis.tutorial: A short, jargon-free walkthrough of how the locking and unlocking actually works.

vault.totp.what1: Time-based One-Time Password — the rotating 6-digit codes used for two-factor authentication on sites like GitHub or Google.
vault.totp.what2: When a site offers 2FA, it shows a QR code or a Base32 secret like JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP. Paste that secret here and SecureVault will generate the codes for you — no separate authenticator app needed.

keys.hint: Your public key is safe to share. Your private key is encrypted with your master passphrase — never give that file plus your passphrase to anyone. Back up private_key.asc somewhere safe.
keys.what.title: What is a keyserver?
keys.what.1: A directory on the internet where people publish their public PGP keys so others can find them by email. SecureVault uses keys.openpgp.org, the modern verifying keyserver.
keys.what.2: Publishing requires email confirmation (a verification link is sent to the address on your key). Once verified, anyone can fetch your key by email.
keys.searchByEmail: Search a contact's key by email
keys.verifyBeforeTrust: Verify this fingerprint with your contact through a separate channel before trusting the key.
keys.emailMismatch: This key does not list the email you searched ({0}). Only add it if you trust where it came from.
keys.noneFound: No published key found for that email on keys.openpgp.org.
keys.directoryBody: Public keys of people you can send locked files to. "Add to my contact directory" above copies your own public key here so you can encrypt files for yourself.
keys.emptyBody: Import a public key from someone you trust, or publish your own to encrypt files for yourself.

keys.publishBody1: Your public key will be uploaded so people can find it by email. After uploading, keys.openpgp.org will send a verification email to {0}. Click the link in that email to make your key searchable.
keys.publishBody2: This action only uploads the PUBLIC key. Your private key never leaves your device.

tl.intro: A 2-minute, plain-language walkthrough of how your vault keeps things locked — no tech background needed.
tl.publicDesc: Share it freely. It is only used to encrypt data destined for you.
tl.privateDesc: Keep it secret. Only this key can decrypt what was locked with your public key.
tl.s1.title: You get two keys
tl.s1.body: When you create an account, SecureVault generates two keys that belong only to you. Think of a mailbox: anyone can drop a letter in, only you have the key to take letters out.
tl.s2.title: Your passphrase guards the private key
tl.s2.body: The private key file on disk is itself encrypted with your master passphrase. No passphrase, no access — not even to us. Without it, the file is useless, even if someone copies it.
tl.s3.title: Locking a message
tl.s3.body: To send you something private, someone locks it with your public key. From that moment only your private key can open it.
tl.s4.title: The whole vault is locked too
tl.s4.body: Your passwords, notes and cards are stored as one scrambled blob. On disk it looks like meaningless noise until you unlock it. SecureVault uses a hybrid scheme: a strong random AES-256 key (encrypted with your PGP public key) does the bulk symmetric encryption per field, and the vault as a whole is PGP-wrapped on save.
tl.s5.title: Pick a passphrase you can keep
tl.s6.title: The key directory
tl.s6.body: To encrypt a file for someone else, you need their public key. The Key management page lets you import public keys from people you trust so you can lock files addressed to them.
tl.tip1: Length wins. A 4-word passphrase like caballo correcto batería grapa is much stronger than P@ss1! and far easier to remember.
tl.tip2: Never reuse it. If a website you use is breached and you share passphrases, attackers get your vault too.
tl.tip3: Don't write it down digitally. Pen and paper in a locked drawer is fine.
tl.tip4: It is not recoverable. If you forget it, nobody — including us — can decrypt your vault.
tl.tip5: Back up the private key file. Copy private_key.asc to an offline drive.
